pharm: Stimulates rapid, glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta-cells by closing the ATP-sensitive potassium channel, targeting postprandial glucose when taken before meals.

No adjustment in mild; use caution in moderate-to-severe (not studied)
Limit; alcohol can increase hypoglycemia risk
summary: Nateglinide (Starlix) is a meglitinide, a rapid-acting insulin secretagogue used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release within about 20 minutes and is taken 1 to 30 minutes before each main meal to blunt the postprandial glucose rise. The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can be severe, cause seizures, and be life-threatening; patients should take it before meals and skip the dose if they skip a meal. It is not for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

dosage.t: 1 to 30 minutes before each main meal

dosage.d: 60 mg three times daily before meals
dosage.t: 1 to 30 minutes before each main meal

admin: Take 1 to 30 minutes before each main meal
If a meal is skipped, skip that dose to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia
Use 60 mg three times daily if the patient is near glycemic goal at initiation; otherwise 120 mg three times daily
Educate patients and caregivers to recognize and treat hypoglycemia
Self-monitoring of blood glucose is essential, more frequently in patients at higher hypoglycemia risk
moa: Nateglinide lowers blood glucose by stimulating insulin secretion from the pancreas, an action that depends on functioning beta-cells. It interacts with the ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel on pancreatic beta-cells; the resulting depolarization opens calcium channels, producing calcium influx and insulin release. Insulin secretion is glucose-dependent and diminishes at low glucose levels, and the drug is highly tissue selective with low affinity for heart and skeletal muscle. Because it acts rapidly and briefly, it primarily targets postprandial (meal-related) hyperglycemia.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to nateglinide or any of its inactive ingredients
relative: Renal or hepatic impairment (higher risk of hypoglycemia)
Conditions or drugs that reduce awareness of hypoglycemia (e.g., beta-blockers, autonomic neuropathy)

preg: Available human data are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Animal studies showed no teratogenicity in rats and rabbits at approximately 27 and 8 times the maximum recommended human dose. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy itself carries maternal and fetal risk.
lact: There are no data on the presence of nateglinide in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production; the drug is present in animal milk (milk-to-plasma ratio of unchanged drug about 2.2 in rats). Because of the potential for hypoglycemia in a breastfed infant, use of nateglinide is not recommended while breastfeeding.
renal: No dosage adjustment is recommended for mild to severe renal impairment. Patients with moderate-to-severe impairment (CrCl 15-50 mL/min) not on dialysis show similar clearance, AUC, and Cmax to healthy subjects. In end-stage renal disease, the active M1 metabolite may accumulate and could increase hypoglycemic effect, so patients with renal impairment may be at higher risk of hypoglycemia.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is recommended for mild hepatic impairment (Cmax and AUC increased about 37% and 30%). Use in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment has not been studied; use with caution as these patients may be at higher risk of hypoglycemia.

major: Other antidiabetic agents and insulin - additive hypoglycemia risk
moderate: Drugs that increase glucose-lowering effect / hypoglycemia: NSAIDs, salicylates, MAO inhibitors, non-selective beta-blockers, anabolic hormones, guanethidine, and CYP2C9 inhibitors (amiodarone, fluconazole, voriconazole, sulfinpyrazone), alcohol - may need dose reduction and more frequent glucose monitoring

Drugs that reduce glucose-lowering effect / cause hyperglycemia: thiazides, corticosteroids, thyroid products, sympathomimetics, somatropin, somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide), and CYP inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, St John's Wort) - may need dose increase and more frequent monitoring
Drugs that blunt signs of hypoglycemia: beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine, reserpine - monitor glucose more frequently
minor: No clinically relevant interaction was seen with glyburide, metformin, digoxin, warfarin, or diclofenac
interactions.food: Take 1 to 30 minutes before meals; absorption is more consistent when taken before a meal, and peak levels are lower if taken too long before a liquid meal.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may increase the blood-glucose-lowering effect and risk of hypoglycemia; limit intake.
interactions.diagnostics: Postmarketing reports of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis, and elevated liver enzymes; modest increases in serum uric acid observed.

serious: Cholestatic hepatitis / jaundice / elevated liver enzymes (postmarketing)
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia - can cause seizures, may be life-threatening or cause death; treat hypoglycemia with loss of consciousness or neurological symptoms with intravenous glucose

monitoring: Self-monitoring of blood glucose, with increased frequency in patients at higher hypoglycemia risk
Liver enzymes if hepatobiliary symptoms occur
counsel: Take this medicine 1 to 30 minutes before your main meals
If you skip a meal, skip that dose to avoid low blood sugar
Learn the signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) and how to treat it with fast-acting sugar
Low blood sugar can happen suddenly and may impair driving or operating machinery
Tell your clinician about all other medicines, since many can raise or lower your blood sugar
Continue your diet, exercise, and regular blood glucose monitoring
pk: Stimulates insulin secretion within about 20 minutes of dosing
Peak plasma concentration within about 1 hour (peak insulin about 1 hour after a pre-meal dose)
Insulin levels fall to baseline by about 4 hours; dosed three times daily with meals
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); dispense in a tight, light-resistant container
pearls: Rapid, short-acting prandial secretagogue - take just before meals and skip the dose if the meal is skipped
Hypoglycemia is the main risk and can be severe; risk is higher in renal or hepatic impairment and with interacting drugs
Beta-blockers and other sympatholytics can mask hypoglycemia warning signs
Metabolized mainly by CYP2C9 (and CYP3A4); CYP2C9 inhibitors increase hypoglycemia risk while inducers reduce efficacy
Not for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis; modest weight gain may occur
missed: Nateglinide is taken with meals. If you forget a dose at a meal, do not take an extra dose later - simply take your next dose before your next meal. If you skip a meal, skip that dose. Do not double up.
overdose: An overdose may cause an exaggerated glucose-lowering effect with hypoglycemia. Treat hypoglycemic symptoms without loss of consciousness or neurological findings with oral glucose and adjust dose and/or meal patterns. Treat severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure, or other neurological symptoms with intravenous glucose. Because nateglinide is highly protein bound, dialysis is not an effective means of removal.
